title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: Build a governed semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with the Denodo Platform and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It federates Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and an on-premises PostgreSQL database into a single customer 360 view an agent queries in VQL, with identity propagation and row- and column-level access control enforced at the semantic layer.
content:
Agentic AI applications need governed access to live enterprise data. That data can live in operational systems, analytical warehouses, SaaS applications, other clouds, or on premises. In the previous post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. A Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore queried that layer. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post uses the same customer 360 pattern, but swaps in a different semantic layer implementation and extends the source mix.
Two things change here. First, the semantic layer is the Denodo Platform: an AI data layer that provides active context and live, zero-copy access to distributed enterprise data. The agent talks to it in VQL , Denodo’s SQL dialect. Second, the source mix includes an on-premises PostgreSQL database alongside Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift, so the federation problem is no longer bounded by an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC).
The rest of the pattern carries over. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock plans and writes queries. The Denodo MCP Server exposes governed views to the agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent, terminates inbound authentication, and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to Denodo. Everything the model reasons over lives inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt: the joins, the metric definitions, and the row and column filters that apply to the caller.
By the end of this post, you will know:

How to federate Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and an on-premises PostgreSQL database in Denodo into a single customer 360 view an agent can query.
How to expose that semantic view to an AgentCore-hosted agent through the Denodo MCP Server, and how to register the MCP Server as an AgentCore Gateway target.
How the end user’s identity flows from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity On-Behalf-Of token exchange to Denodo.
How Global Security Policies apply row and column filters at query time.
The two deployment options for Denodo on AWS: Agora , the fully managed cloud service, and self-managed installation on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS).

We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the previous post: what it is, what it’s for, and why the model plans query without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the previous post covers the ground.
The example: Customer 360 with a source outside AWS
We stay with the same customer 360 pattern from the previous post. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit used in the previous article models an ecommerce retailer with two motivating use cases: understanding churn and identifying customers for auto-enrollment in a rewards program. The schema doesn’t change in this post. What changes is where one table lives: rewards_account sits on an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster rather than in Amazon Aurora with the rest of the customer profile data.
That placement isn’t a special case. Enterprise data sources might be outside AWS: on premises, in a SaaS tool like a CRM, or in another cloud. The semantic layer must reach whichever applies. We use on-premises PostgreSQL for the walkthrough that represents data from a third-party application. The Extending to other sources section covers what changes when the source is a SaaS tool, a CRM, or a mainframe. It also covers the other hundreds of data sources that Denodo supports by default .
Amazon Aurora (PostgreSQL-compatible): Customer profile

Table
Key columns

customer
cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location

address
id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name

credit_card
id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type

Amazon Redshift: Order history

Table
Key columns

order
id (PK), cid, pid, order_date, quantity, price, card

product
id (PK), name, brand, price, dept

On-premises PostgreSQL: Rewards program

Table
Key columns

rewards_account
id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date

The shared identifier is cid , a plain integer that appears as the primary key in the Aurora customer table. It appears as a non-foreign-key column in the Amazon Redshift order table and the on-premises rewards_account . Within Aurora itself, the customer.location column is an integer foreign key to address.id , which is how the profile joins to the address record. There is no foreign key that spans two engines, and no ETL job to build one. Answers that join customers to their purchases and their rewards enrollment must reconcile cid at query time.
A representative question this setup answers: “Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?” This is the auto-enrollment scenario from the Stardog kit, and it needs profile data from Aurora, lifetime spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from the on-premises cluster to answer.
Denodo plans the federated query at execution time, deciding what to push into Aurora, what to push into Amazon Redshift, what to fetch from the on-premises cluster, and how to combine the results. No data moves between sources, and the semantic layer stays declared once for every consumer to reuse.
Denodo terms used in this post
Denodo implements the semantic layer as a data virtualization platform. Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) is the query engine at the core: it’s where the semantic-layer objects live, where VQL executes, and where access policies evaluate. Design Studio is the browser-based authoring surface for VDP. Every object modeled in this post is defined there.
Three object types come up repeatedly.

A base view is a mapping between a physical table, API, or file in a source system and a logical view in VDP. One Aurora table maps to one base view.
A derived view is a VQL query over one or more base or other derived views. The customer_360 view in this post is a derived view.
A metric view defines a business measure once (for example, lifetime_customer_value ) and lets other derived views reference it. Metric views separate the definition of a measure from any specific query that uses it.

VQL is Denodo’s SQL dialect. It’s ANSI-aligned SQL plus a set of Denodo-specific constructs, notably DDL constructs to represent data sources and syntax for semantic metric views. In an agentic scenario, the specific syntax of VQL is provided by a skill that will be used by the LLM when using Denodo tools to facilitate correct use of Denodo’s syntax.
A Global Security Policy (GSP) is a runtime access-control rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag. GSPs are how row filters and column masks get enforced at query time, evaluated per caller.
For a fuller reference, see the Denodo Platform documentation .
Reference architecture
The runtime has two flows. Inbound: A client sends the user’s request to the agent through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process. The agent invokes a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in this walkthrough) to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound: AgentCore Gateway also acts as the outbound proxy for the agent’s tool calls. The Denodo MCP Server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls the agent makes for enterprise data route through Gateway to the MCP Server. Before the request reaches Denodo, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange , converting the human user’s inbound token into a scoped access token that represents the same user with Denodo as the audience. The Denodo MCP Server accepts the exchanged token as a bearer credential and forwards the VQL request to Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) over JDBC. VDP validates the token independently, resolves the caller to a Denodo role, applies access policies, and plans the federated query against Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL cluster.
Only the VQL request travels down to VDP and the result set travels back up. No source data moves between engines. Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises cluster respond to native SQL rewritten by VDP’s federated optimizer. The following sections cover the identity propagation and policy enforcement in detail. Additional sections cover the MCP Server registration and agent deployment steps.

Figure 1: Inbound authentication path and outbound query path between the caller, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components, the Denodo MCP Server, Denodo Virtual DataPort, and the three data sources

Build the semantic layer
The semantic model in Denodo is not a single artifact. It’s a collection of base views, derived views, metric views, and tags in VDP that together present business-meaningful data to consumers. Building the semantic model in this post means creating each of those pieces.
We build in three passes: base views over each source table, a derived view ( customer_360 ) that joins the base views on cid at the customer level, and a metric view ( lifetime_customer_value ) that defines a reusable spend aggregation queries can join in when they need it.
In practice, this modeling is done visually in Denodo Design Studio. You drag Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL source onto a canvas, draw joins between them, and rename or re-type fields (for example, mapping cust_ref to customer_id ) through a form rather than hand-written DDL. Attaching the security policies covered later in this post also happens inside the same UI.
Metric views live beside the derived views that reference them, defined once and reused. If two teams build two different customer-level views over the same base data, both surface the same metric definitions.
Base views
Each source table becomes a base view in VDP. For the Aurora customer table, that means introducing Aurora using the specific connector in Design Studio, pointing at the schema, and letting VDP introspect the columns. Design Studio handles the introspection. The resulting base view is a one-to-one mapping between the physical columns and their VDP counterparts, and it doesn’t transform the source data.
Two additional configurations happen during creation:

Column tags for governance. ssn on the base view over customer gets the tag pii_sensitive . card_num on the base view over credit_card gets the same tag. These tags are what the Global Security Policy defined in the Governed access section binds to.
Primary keys and join fields. cid is marked as the primary key on aurora_customer and as the join field on redshift_order and postgres_rewards_account . Design Studio infers primary keys from source metadata when it’s available. Otherwise, you set them once in the base view definition.

Repeat for the source tables introduced earlier. Six base views result: aurora_customer , aurora_address , and aurora_credit_card over Amazon Aurora; redshift_order and redshift_product over Amazon Redshift; and postgres_rewards_account over on-premises PostgreSQL.
Design Studio also supports natural-language authoring through Denodo Assistant . A developer can describe a view in plain English (for example, “join customer profile from Aurora with order totals from Amazon Redshift on cid ”) and get back a candidate VQL definition to review and refine in the same canvas before saving. Refinement is iterative: follow-up prompts adjust filters, joins, or field mappings before the definition is finalized. The governance and typing rules described in this section still apply to objects created this way.
Derived view: The customer 360
customer_360 is the customer-level view across the three sources, with one row per customer. Order details and aggregations live separately, in the metric view we define next.

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW customer_360 AS
SELECT aurora_customer.cid,
aurora_customer.first_name,
aurora_customer.last_name,
aurora_customer.email,
aurora_customer.ssn,
aurora_address.city,
aurora_address.state,
aurora_credit_card.card_num,
aurora_credit_card.card_type,
postgres_rewards_account.account_id,
postgres_rewards_account.create_date AS rewards_since
FROM (
(
aurora_customer AS aurora_customer
LEFT OUTER JOIN aurora_address AS aurora_address
ON aurora_customer.location = aurora_address.id
)
LEFT OUTER JOIN aurora_credit_card AS aurora_credit_card
ON aurora_customer.cid = aurora_credit_card.cid
)
LEFT OUTER JOIN postgres_rewards_account AS postgres_rewards_account
ON aurora_customer.cid = postgres_rewards_account.cid;

Two properties of this definition matter for the rest of the architecture. First, the joins live in Denodo Platform rather than in a pipeline. There is no ETL job maintaining a materialized customer_360 table. VDP resolves the joins at execution time: Aurora returns the profile plus card, the on-premises cluster returns the rewards enrollment record, and VDP combines them on cid . Second, the derived view carries every column, including ssn and card_num .
For governance and AI, we also add metadata: column tags for personally identifiable information (PII) fields, and descriptions that document the view and each field. Denodo’s Assistant can use an LLM to suggest these. Later sections show why this metadata matters.

Figure 2: The customer_360 derived view in Denodo Design Studio. Four base views appear on the canvas across the three sources, joined on cid and location. The ssn column on aurora_customer and the card_num column on aurora_credit_card carry the pii_sensitive tag referenced by the Global Security Policy in the Governed access section

Metric view: Lifetime customer value
Metric views define reusable business measures with a specific SOURCES/DIMENSIONS/METRICS structure. See the Defining a Metric View reference in the VQL guide for the full syntax. lifetime_customer_value doesn’t live inside customer_360 . It lives beside it, as its own object:

CREATE OR REPLACE METRIC VIEW lifetime_customer_value
(
first_name, last_name, state, rewards_since, lifetime_spend, order_count, product_id,product_name, product_brand,product_dept, units_sold
)
SOURCES (
customer_360 AS customer_360,
redshift_order AS redshift_order,
redshift_product AS redshift_product
)
ASSOCIATIONS (
customer_360 redshift_order assoc_customer360_orders,
redshift_product redshift_order assoc_product_orders
)
DIMENSIONS (
customer_360(
first_name AS customer_360.first_name,
last_name AS customer_360.last_name,
state AS customer_360.state,
rewards_since AS customer_360.rewards_since
),
product(
product_id AS redshift_product.id,
product_name AS redshift_product.name,
product_brand AS redshift_product.brand,
product_dept AS redshift_product.dept
)
)
METRICS (
lifetime_spend AS sum((redshift_order.price*redshift_order.quantity)),
order_count AS count(redshift_order.id),
units_sold AS sum(redshift_order.quantity)
);

Other views and external reporting tools can reference lifetime_customer_value the same way it references other views. When a business rule changes (say, lifetime_spend should exclude canceled orders), the update happens once in the metric definition. Every consumer picks up the change at the next query, without touching the derived view or the downstream application. Different teams can stand up their own derived views to convey the way their line of business sees the world. The base data stays shared while the semantic interpretation stays independent, so neither team’s edits disturb the other.

Figure 3: The lifetime_customer_value metric view in Design Studio, showing the SOURCES, DIMENSIONS, and METRICS panels that define lifetime_spend, order_count, and units_sold

How VDP executes the federated query
When the agent runs the auto-enrollment question from The example ( “Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?” ), the corresponding VQL uses the metric view to compute the result set and evaluate the desired metric:

SELECT first_name, last_name, state, EVALUATE_METRIC(lifetime_spend) AS lifetime_spend
FROM lifetime_customer_value
WHERE rewards_since IS NULL
GROUP BY first_name, last_name, state
ORDER BY EVALUATE_METRIC(lifetime_spend) DESC
LIMIT 20;

Although this query only references the metric view, VDP’s cost-based optimizer plans the federated execution across the three engines where the corresponding data is originating. The resulting plan looks approximately like this:

Push down to Amazon Aurora : Denodo pushes a join of customer, address, and credit_card to Aurora, returning customer profile fields including first_name , last_name , state, and cid .
Push down to on-premises PostgreSQL : Denodo pushes a projection of rewards_account returning cid and create_date .
Push down to Amazon Redshift : Denodo pushes the spend aggregation to Amazon Redshift as SUM(price * quantity) grouped by cid .
Combine inside Denodo : Denodo left-joins the Aurora profile result with the PostgreSQL rewards result on cid , then right-outer-joins that result with the Amazon Redshift aggregated spend on cid . Denodo filters rows where rewards_since IS NULL, evaluates the metric as the outer grouped aggregation ( sum(sum) AS lifetime_spend ) grouped by first_name , last_name , and state, orders by lifetime_spend descending, and returns up to 20 rows.

The plan reflects the strengths of each source. Amazon Redshift does the aggregation, Aurora does the customer-profile join because all three profile tables live there, and the on-premises cluster returns a small set of rewards records. VDP handles the final cross-engine join and the top-N filter, working with three compact intermediate result sets that carry one row per customer rather than one row per order. A hand-written pipeline usually approximates this same shape and then must keep it in sync forever.
VDP also handles type reconciliation where it’s cheapest. If the same identifier is stored as an integer in one source and a string in another, VDP pushes the cast into the source that can still filter on the resulting predicate, rather than pulling data across engines and reconciling types afterward.

Figure 4: The query flow from the C360 agent to Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and on-premises PostgreSQL and back. VDP rewrites one VQL request against customer_360 joined with lifetime_customer_value into source-native SQL per engine, collects the intermediate result sets, and joins them on cid inside VDP before returning the final rows to the agent

Beyond query push-down and on-demand federation, VDP also offers caching, aggregate-aware acceleration, and point-to-point replication . These techniques complement push-down capabilities in use cases where pre-calculating complex transformations may be necessary, while preserving access control rules and data lineage.
Publish for discovery
A semantic view that only exists as a queryable endpoint leaves a discoverability gap. The next team that needs a “ customer lifetime value ” measure has no way to know lifetime_customer_value already exists, what it’s built on, or who else depends on it. Publishing customer_360 and lifetime_customer_value to the Denodo Data Marketplace turns them into reusable, governed enterprise data products and closes that gap: both objects appear with their VQL definitions, ownership, business descriptions, custom properties, and lineage back to the base views. Consumers search by business meaning rather than by knowing the schema. The Denodo Data Marketplace also provides other features focused on self-service for non-technical users, including data preparation wizards, endorsements and deprecations notes from the administrators, and the capability to make requests and ask questions to data product owners.
Denodo extends this with the 360 graph , a relationship view around a business concept. This graph attaches the reports, dashboards, notebooks, or agent tools that already use customer_360 , along with glossaries that define the meaning of the data in the table or conditions of use, for instance. Consumers can inspect the surrounding context of the dataset before writing a query.

Figure 5: customer_360 graph view listing in the Denodo Data Marketplace. The detail panel shows a BI tool in Tableau consuming the view and the glossary definition linked to the view

A note on interoperability
The semantic model in Denodo is defined in VQL, but Denodo natively exposes any view over multiple open protocols. The same customer_360 view can be reached as SQL through JDBC, ODBC, or ADBC, as GraphQL through the Denodo GraphQL Service, as OData 2.0 or 4.0 through the Denodo OData Service, or as MCP tools through the Denodo MCP Server. Choosing MCP for this walkthrough is a fit for AgentCore. The same view is available to a Power BI dashboard, a Tableau workbook, or a Java application without additional modeling.
Denodo also joined Apache Ossie (incubating), formerly Open Semantic Interchange (OSI), in March 2026, a vendor-neutral open-source specification for semantic metadata. Apache Ossie is at an early stage, but the intent is portability of semantic definitions across applications that adopt it. That said, Denodo already offers integration through Denodo Connects to share metadata with other data catalogs such as SageMaker Catalog, Collibra, Purview, and others.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Broad reach across data sources is one of the core characteristics of an enterprise-wide semantic layer, but that same reach creates a real risk when runtime access control is missing. If per-user filtering lives in the agent’s code, it’s one prompt injection away from being bypassed. If it lives in the LLM, it doesn’t really live anywhere. If it is enforced only in individual source systems, policies can be inconsistent and may not account for business meaning created across sources. Aurora doesn’t know what “ top spender ” means in the semantic layer, and neither does an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster behind a bastion host. And very often, especially in hybrid scenarios that blend on-premises and cloud systems, Identity Providers across all of them are not even an option.
The approach in this architecture is to enforce access at the semantic layer, using the identity of the human user who initiated the request, propagated end-to-end from the IdP through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to Denodo Virtual DataPort.
The identity propagation chain
Figure 6 zooms into the identity portion of the reference architecture in Figure 1, expanding the outbound path from the app to Denodo VDP into an eight-hop sequence. The following numbered steps correspond one-to-one to the numbered arrows in the figure.

Figure 6: Identity propagation and query flow from the user’s login through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to Denodo (MCP Server and VDP) and the underlying data sources. Black arrows show the outbound identity and query path. Green dashed arrows show the return path with the filtered result set

The user authenticates to the app against the enterprise IdP. The IdP returns a JWT carrying the user’s identity and attribute claims — role, region, department, and whatever else the IdP is configured to emit.
The app calls the agent through AgentCore Gateway with the user’s JWT as the bearer token.
Gateway routes the request to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process.
When the agent invokes an outbound tool call, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange and returns a new access token whose sub claim is the human user and whose aud claim is Denodo.
The agent presents the new access token to the Denodo MCP Server as Authorization: Bearer <access_token> on the MCP request.
Denodo VDP validates the JWT against the configured JWKS URL, checks the issuer and audience, extracts the scope claim, and maps the caller to a Denodo role.
VDP evaluates Global Security Policies at query time and returns a filtered result set to the agent.
VDP queries the data sources to satisfy the request and combines the results before returning them.

Gateway JWT validation at step 2 is optional because VDP re-validates the token in step 6. With Gateway validation on, malformed tokens fail earlier in the request path.
The token exchange at step 4 uses either the RFC 8693 token-exchange grant or the RFC 7523 JWT-bearer grant, based on the credential provider configuration. The credential itself does not enter agent code. AgentCore Identity injects it at call time.
The caller-identity passthrough option at step 8 is enabled per data source and requires Denodo and the source to share the same IdP. When it applies, the caller’s identity is forwarded end-to-end, giving full auditing at the source.
Applying access policies in Denodo
Customer 360 data is regulated. For example, some users (HR, fraud analysts) may need to see PII like a Social Security number (SSN) and full credit card number. But most users (marketing, analytics) must not.
Denodo’s mechanism for this is Global Security Policies with attribute- and role-based access control. A Global Security Policy is a rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag, evaluated against the caller’s role and session attributes at query time. The underlying view is not restructured.
To illustrate this, we’ve tagged two columns ( ssn and card_num ) as PII on the base views over Aurora. We create a Global Security Policy mask_pii_columns .

Audience: The caller’s role is not hr_user .
Elements: Applies to columns with the pii_sensitive tag.
Action: Mask with asterisks ( **** ).

We then define two Denodo roles.

hr_user : Has Execute on customer_360 . Sees every column.
marketing_user : Has Execute on customer_360 . Will see ssn and card_num as **** because the policy applies.

When marketing_user runs the VQL query:

SELECT cid, first_name, last_name, state, ssn
FROM customer_360
WHERE state = 'WI';

VDP evaluates the Global Security Policy before planning the query. It sees that ssn carries the pii_sensitive tag and the caller’s role is not hr_user , so it rewrites the projection to return *** for ssn .
For row-level filtering (a US-East analyst who should only see east-coast customers, for example) the same mechanism scales. The policy condition can even depend on session attributes mapped from the JWT token, or pulled dynamically from an external table.
A note on Responsible AI
Denodo’s Global Security Policies filter PII at the semantic layer, so the model never sees ssn or card_num for callers who shouldn’t. Even then, agent responses can echo customer identifiers, locations, or spending patterns in natural language. Treat agent outputs with the same handling and retention policy you apply to the underlying regulated data: scope logging and transcript storage, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content and sensitive-topic controls, and limit who can read the responses. For broader guidance, see Responsible AI in Amazon Bedrock .
Audit and observability across layers
Each layer of the request path logs independently. AgentCore runtime emits invocation records to Amazon CloudWatch . AgentCore Gateway logs inbound MCP requests, including the caller’s JWT sub claim. The Denodo MCP Server records tool calls to its own log. Denodo VDP’s audit log captures the full VQL request, the mapped Denodo role, the resolved federated plan, and policy evaluation outcomes.
These logs can also be incorporated into Amazon CloudWatch . When per-source audit tied to the human user is required (for HIPAA or SOX compliance, for example), configure pass-through session credentials on the base views for those sources so Denodo forwards the caller’s identity to the source system where the source supports it, instead of relying on service accounts.
Expose the layer through the Denodo MCP Server
The Denodo MCP Server is an add-on component that sits between MCP clients and VDP: download the distribution, extract it, edit config/application.properties , and start it. The server listens for streamable HTTP MCP requests at http://<mcp-host>:8080/<database>/mcp and forwards them to VDP over JDBC.
Three configuration values matter for this walkthrough.

mcp.security.oauth2.enabled=true : accepts OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens on inbound MCP requests. Paired with VDP’s OAuth authenticator configuration, the token forwards to VDP for validation and role resolution (see also the Governed access section).
vdp.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:vdb://<vdp-host>:9999/ : the JDBC URL where VDP is reached. The specific database targeted per request comes from the MCP endpoint path.
mcp.visibility.tags=mcp controls which views are visible from the MCP Server. If defined, only views tagged with at least one of these tags will be visible.

The server implements the MCP OAuth 2.0 authorization flow, including RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata and RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration.
A note on IdP compatibility
The Denodo MCP Server documents support for the automatic Dynamic Client Registration flow with Okta, Ping Identity, and Keycloak. For other identity providers, the MCP Server also accepts manual client configuration where the OAuth token is obtained out of band and forwarded as a static Authorization header on the MCP request, as described in the Denodo MCP Server User Manual .
Front the server with an Application Load Balancer
If the Denodo MCP Server runs on Amazon EC2 or Amazon EKS in the same VPC as VDP, expose it through an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager . This gives AgentCore Gateway a stable HTTPS endpoint and offloads TLS termination from the MCP Server process. Target group: HTTP, port 8080. The health check path should accept both 200 and 404 as healthy responses, since the root path returns 404 and /health returns 200 when the server is up and connected to VDP.
Register as an AgentCore Gateway target
The full step-by-step walkthrough, including AgentCore Gateway creation, IAM service role configuration, and Gateway target validation, is in Denodo’s Integrating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Denodo via MCP Server integration guide.
Add Denodo VQL skill in the harness
The Denodo VQL skill acts as a system prompt extension for the LLM within the agent framework (such as Strands or Bedrock AgentCore). When registered in the agent harness, it instructs the model on VQL syntax rules and how to help prevent SQL errors.
Deploy and run the agent
The Denodo AgentCore documentation reference has the full agent code in the Denodo KB. The pattern is short: a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock, an MCP client pointed at the Denodo MCP Server, and an AgentCore runtime entrypoint that wires them together.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we run three query categories through the agent, plus one governance rerun that demonstrates the same-query-two-users property from the Governed access section. We can use Denodo’s Data Marketplace assistant, which relies on equivalent tools behind the scenes, to get a quick validation on our scenario.
Query 1, Aurora-only
“List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.”
The agent generates and runs:

/* The query needs to retrieve first_name, last_name, and city from the customer_360 view where state = 'WI', ordered by last_name. The output will be multiple rows with 3 columns. The table is at customer granularity (one row per customer). No obligatory columns are present, so a simple WHERE filter on state suffices. */
SELECT "first_name",
"last_name",
"city"
FROM "customer_360"."customer_360"
WHERE "state" = 'WI'
ORDER BY "last_name"

VDP’s optimizer determines that only Aurora-side data is needed for the projection and filter, and pushes a single query down to Amazon Aurora. Based on a probe query, the agent can translate the filter from Wisconsin to the predicate state = 'WI' . Amazon Redshift and the on-premises cluster are not touched.
Query 2, Redshift-only
“What are our top 10 products by units sold?”
The agent generates:

/* The user wants top 10 products by total units sold from a metric view. I need to use EVALUATE_METRIC for units_sold, GROUP BY product_name, ORDER BY the metric descending, LIMIT 10. The output will be multiple rows (up to 10) with two columns: product_name and total_units_sold. */
SELECT "product_name",
EVALUATE_METRIC("units_sold") AS "total_units_sold"
FROM "customer_360"."lifetime_customer_value"
GROUP BY "product_name"
ORDER BY "total_units_sold" DESC
LIMIT 10

Figure 7: VDP pushes the entire query (join, aggregation, ordering, and limit) to Amazon Redshift because both the product and order data live there. Aurora and the on-premises cluster are not touched

Query 3, three-way federation
“Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime value haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?”
The agent generates:

/* This is a metric view, so I need to use EVALUATE_METRIC for lifetime_spend and order_count. The query needs to: 1. Aggregate by first_name, last_name, state, rewards_since to get total lifetime_spend and order_count 2. Rank top 20 by total lifetime_spend 3. Filter those top 20 where rewards_since IS NULL I'll use a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() to get top 20, then filter for NULL rewards_since in outer query. */
WITH "ranked_customers" AS (
SELECT "first_name",
"last_name",
"state",
"rewards_since",
EVALUATE_METRIC("lifetime_spend") AS "total_lifetime_spend",
EVALUATE_METRIC("order_count") AS "total_order_count"
FROM "customer_360"."lifetime_customer_value"
GROUP BY "first_name",
"last_name",
"state",
"rewards_since"
ORDER BY "total_lifetime_spend" DESC
LIMIT 20
)
SELECT "first_name",
"last_name",
"state",
"rewards_since",
"total_lifetime_spend",
"total_order_count"
FROM "ranked_customers"
WHERE "rewards_since" IS NULL
ORDER BY "total_lifetime_spend" DESC

Figure 8: Agent result for the three-way federated query, listing the top customers by lifetime value who have not enrolled in the rewards program

VDP plans across the three engines as described in the Build the semantic layer section: profile from Aurora, aggregated spend from Amazon Redshift, enrollment records from the on-premises cluster, and the final join and top-N inside VDP. The top result in the POC data was Marcus Chen from Milwaukee, WI, with $47,832 in lifetime spend, a customer with high spend and no rewards enrollment, exactly the auto-enrollment target from the example question in The example . Note that the LLM didn’t need to come up with the definition of lifetime_spend , since the formula is part of the semantic model as defined in the metric view.
Governance rerun
We run Query 1 with ssn added to the projection, as two different callers:

SELECT cid, first_name, last_name, state, ssn
FROM customer_360
WHERE state = 'WI';

As hr_user , the result includes the ssn values. As marketing_user , the result returns the same rows with ssn with asterisks as a masked value. No changes to the query text, the agent code, the MCP Server, VDP, or Aurora between the two runs. The Global Security Policy mask_pii_columns from the Governed access section evaluates against the caller’s role at query time, and VDP rewrites the projection accordingly. The same behavior applies to card_num .

Figure 9: The governance rerun of the same query, with ssn returned in full for hr_user and masked for marketing_user

Extending to other sources
Adding a source outside AWS to customer_360 , whether that’s Salesforce for CRM records, ServiceNow for customer service data, or SAP for ERP tables, is the same modeling exercise as Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises cluster. Create a base view, join it into the derived view on cid , and tag sensitive columns. The metric views, the Global Security Policy, and the agent’s VQL don’t change. What changes is the wrapper VDP uses to reach the source. For example:

Salesforce connects through the Denodo Salesforce connector with OAuth 2.0 authentication and VQL-to-SOQL translation over the REST or Bulk API.
ServiceNow, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and other SaaS tools use Denodo’s SaaS wizard templates , pre-configured for common APIs.
SAP ERP connects through BAPI sources using the SAP Java Connector. VDP calls SAP RFCs and shapes the response into rows.

The agent doesn’t know which of these sits underneath. It queries customer_360 in VQL. Denodo’s wrapper handles the source-native translation, and Denodo’s Global Security Policy applies uniformly whether the row comes from a JDBC engine, a REST API, or an RFC call.
One deployment-time decision varies by source: whether to pass the caller’s identity through to the source or connect as a service account. Pass-through gives end-to-end audit at the source when the source supports it (Kerberos to SAP or OAuth to Salesforce, for example). Service-account connections are simpler, and the source’s audit shows the query as coming from Denodo.
Deployment: Denodo Agora versus self-managed
Denodo on AWS runs in one of two shapes. Both use the same Virtual DataPort, same VQL, same Global Security Policies, same MCP Server. The choice is operational.
Agora: Fully managed
Denodo Agora is Denodo’s fully managed cloud service, available on the AWS Marketplace . Agora runs on a split-plane architecture. The Control Plane (Solution Manager, Design Studio, Scheduler admin, Monitoring/Diagnostics) runs in Denodo’s cloud accounts, and the Execution Plane (VDP, Scheduler, Data Catalog) runs inside the customer’s AWS account. The compute that touches the data lives in the customer’s VPC. The management surface is operated by Denodo.
Choose Agora when you don’t want to operate the application and the update cadence Denodo publishes works for your organization.
Self-managed on Amazon EC2 or Amazon EKS
Self-managed deployments install Denodo Platform entirely in the customer’s AWS account. Denodo publishes VM images on AWS Marketplace and ships container images with Helm charts for Amazon EKS. You handle the cluster, upgrades, and backups.
Choose self-managed when compliance requires a specific deployment posture, when you want to control the version cadence, or when the reference architecture calls for a Denodo cluster inside a specific VPC.
Reaching sources outside AWS
Both deployment shapes place VDP in the customer’s AWS account. Reaching an on-premises source is the same problem in both cases: a network path from the VPC that hosts VDP to the on-premises cluster, provisioned through whichever hybrid connectivity option the organization already uses. For SaaS sources like Salesforce or ServiceNow, no additional setup is needed, since the Execution Plane has outbound internet access by default, which is sufficient for OAuth 2.0 authentication and REST API calls.
Conclusion and where to start
Reliable agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that presents business-meaningful data over live source systems, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, Denodo Platform, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles.
The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the underlying databases. Base views, derived views, metric views, tags, and Global Security Policies live in VDP. When a source schema drifts, when a new source comes online, or when a governance rule changes, the update happens in the semantic layer and every consumer picks it up at the next query. The additional metadata the semantic layer carries (documentation, descriptions, metric formulas, and the 360 graph) gives the model more grounded business context to reason over, rather than raw schema alone.
Where to start
Try Agora on AWS and follow the instructions to deploy. Agora is Denodo’s fully managed cloud service for deploying an AI data layer on AWS, providing live, governed access to distributed enterprise data.
Most teams get this working by starting narrow and expanding.

Pick one agentic workflow that spans two or three distinct source systems that takes longer than it should to answer today.
Write three to five specific questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer must support on day one.
Connect data sources and create base views over the source tables the workflow touches. Tag PII columns during creation.
Build the derived views and metric views the questions require.
Implement Global Security Policy to help protect PII, protected health information (PHI), payment card industry (PCI), or other sensitive information.
Register the Denodo MCP Server as an AgentCore Gateway target and wire a Strands agent to it using the pattern in the earlier section. Deploy with agentcore deploy .

title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: The third post in our semantic-layer series builds a customer 360 across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora with Strategy Mosaic, exposes it to a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore through the Mosaic MCP server, and enforces per-user row and column security end-to-end.
content:
This post is co-written with Zhili Cheng, Principal Product Manager, George Earle, Director, AI Engineering, and Kyler K, Sales Engineer of Strategy.
In the first post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift and ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with Strategy Mosaic as the semantic layer.
Stardog’s semantic layer is ontology-based: concepts and relationships modeled as RDF, with IRIs as the unit of federation and SPARQL as the query language. Denodo’s is data virtualization: base and derived views composed in VQL. Mosaic’s is dimensional: attributes, hierarchies, facts, and metrics composed through Strategy’s metric expression syntax, with linked models as the unit of federation. That model serves four native protocols from one definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents, JDBC/ODBC over Trino for SQL clients, XMLA for Power BI and Excel, and REST for custom applications. Behind those protocols is a long list of certified data sources . Supported systems include cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Databricks. Operational databases include Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) , Oracle, and SQL Server. Analytical engines include Amazon Athena , Trino, and SAP HANA, and software as a service (SaaS) sources include Salesforce. The linked-model pattern extends beyond the Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora pair this walkthrough uses. In this walkthrough, a Strands agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, reaches Mosaic through the MCP endpoint. The joins, metric definitions, and per-caller row and column filters live inside Mosaic, not in the agent prompt.
We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series. If any of it is new, the Stardog post covers the ground.
By the end of this post, you will know:

How to model a C360 domain in Strategy Mosaic across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora using two linked models, with no ETL.
How Mosaic’s metric syntax (base, advanced with named filter objects, level qualifiers, and compound) captures the business definitions the agent must reason over.
How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP server, and how user identity propagates so per-user Row-Level Security (RLS) and Object-Level Security (OLS) hold end-to-end.
How to choose between live pushdown and in-memory execution for agent traffic.
How to publish the same governed definitions to Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, and custom apps, and how to export them in Apache Ossie format for tools outside Mosaic.

The source of truth for the walkthrough is Strategy One (March 2026) , the release when Mosaic access through the MCP server became available by default.
Strategy Mosaic terms used in this post
A short reference before we get to the model.

Mosaic Schema and Mosaic Models . Two modeling paths within one universal semantic layer. Mosaic Schema is the centrally governed enterprise model. Mosaic Models is the self-service, AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio. Models can map to Schema attributes and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS. This walkthrough uses Mosaic Models.
Model . The top-level artifact within either modeling path. Publishes attributes, metrics, hierarchies, and security rules over physical tables. The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, one over Amazon Redshift and one over Aurora, linked together.
Attribute . A business entity such as Customer. Carries multiple forms: an ID form for joining and a display form for reading. Mosaic uses forms to resolve names like “Carolyn Inworth” to the underlying cid .
Hierarchy . A parent-child relationship between attributes. Category rolls up through parent to Department. Address rolls up to City to State.
Fact and metric . A fact is a numeric column. A metric aggregates it. Purchase Amount = price * quantity is a base metric. Metrics can also be advanced (an aggregation qualified by a named condition) or compound (a formula over other metrics).
Filter object . A named condition referenced from metrics in angle brackets. [Large Orders] is a filter whose qualification is Purchase Amount > 500 . A metric references <[Large Orders]> without inlining the predicate.
Level qualifier . Metric expression syntax that pins aggregation grain. {~+, !Customer+} sets the grain to Customer regardless of how the query is sliced.
Model linking . Composition across models on shared attributes (Customer, Time). Mosaic pushes aggregates to each source and joins intermediate results on the linking attributes.
Certified model . Only certified models are reachable through the MCP server.
Live or in-memory . Two per-model execution modes: live pushdown to the source, or answers from a Mosaic-resident cube. Details later in this post.

The example: Customer 360 across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora
The C360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. The schema is adapted from Stardog’s C360 Knowledge Kit , so a reader following the series sees the same entities, keys, and anchor question answered by a different semantic layer. A retail organization has customer records, addresses, credit cards, and rewards enrollment sitting on the operational side, and orders, products, and product categories sitting in the warehouse. Business users want answers that span both without knowing which system holds which fact.
Where this post differs is how Mosaic reaches the two sources. Mosaic does not federate rows across engines at query time. It plans one query per source, pushes native SQL down, and joins the intermediate result sets in the Mosaic engine on the shared attributes declared through model linking. The C360 walkthrough models the analytical side as a Purchase model over Amazon Redshift and the operational side as a Customer model over Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible edition.
The schema across the two databases:
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible (operational)

Table
Key columns

customer
cid (PK), first_name , last_name , email , ssn , phone , location

address
id (PK), city , state , zip , street_name

credit_card
id (PK), cid , card_num , card_type

rewards_account
id (PK), cid , account_id , create_date

Amazon Redshift (analytical)

Table
Key columns

purchase
id (PK), cid , pid , date , quantity , price , card

product
id (PK), name , brand , price , dept

category
id (PK), dept_name , parent

vendor
id (PK), vendor_name , industry

The shared ID is cid , an integer that appears as the primary key in customer on Aurora and as a plain column in purchase on Amazon Redshift. There is no SQL constraint linking them, and there can’t be, because they live in different engines. Every question that joins a customer to their orders must reconcile that integer somewhere. Mosaic absorbs it through model linking rather than a materialized cross-engine join.
A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post . It needs customer profile from Aurora, aggregated spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from Aurora, ranked and filtered on definitions that live in the semantic layer.
Reference architecture
Figure 1 shows the end-to-end runtime. The inbound authentication path runs from the client through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the runtime. The outbound query path runs from the Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP endpoint to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora.

Figure 1: Reference architecture. Inbound authentication path and outbound query path between the client, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components, the Strategy Mosaic MCP endpoint, the Mosaic engine, and Amazon Redshift plus Amazon Aurora.

The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path.
Inbound. A client sends the user’s question through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP). It then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent. The agent invokes Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, its MCP tool connects directly to the Mosaic MCP endpoint at https://<env-domain>/collaboration/mcp/mosaic over HTTPS. The agent presents an OAuth 2.0 access token in the Authorization: Bearer header. Mosaic validates the token against its bundled OAuth authorization server and resolves the caller to a Strategy user. It then applies the Use MCP Server privilege and certified-model gate, evaluates row-level and column-level security for that user, and plans the query across the linked Purchase and Customer models. Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora respond to source-native SQL that the Mosaic engine emits per source.
Two properties matter for the rest of the walkthrough. Cross-source joins happen because a modeler declared a link, not because two sources happen to be reachable. The agent can only traverse links that exist in the model. The token that reaches Mosaic represents the human user, not a service account, so RLS and OLS evaluate against the caller’s identity end-to-end. AWS Secrets Manager holds the caller’s refresh token between calls, and the Governed access section walks the full identity chain.
Build the semantic layer
The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, the self-service AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio, linked on shared attributes. Mosaic Studio is the authoring suite, and the screenshots in this post come from its Design Center modeling workspace. Three passes: datasets and joins on each side, attributes and hierarchies, then metrics that carry the business logic. A team with an existing centrally governed Mosaic Schema can map the model’s attributes to it and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS from the enterprise schema without a parallel security review. Do this early if your data architects already maintain a governed schema.
Two linked models
Each Mosaic model connects to one live source. Model linking composes them.

Purchase : Live against Amazon Redshift. Facts on the purchase table ( price * quantity ), dimensions on product , category , vendor , and the purchase date.
Customer : Live against Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible. Dimensions on customer , address , credit_card , rewards_account .

Inside each model, the physical joins are declared once against the source schema. The Purchase model resolves purchase.pid = product.id , product.dept = category.id , and product.brand = vendor.id , plus a self-reference on category.parent = category.id for the department rollup. The Customer model resolves customer.location = address.id , customer.cid = credit_card.cid , and customer.cid = rewards_account.cid . These are the relationships Mosaic uses to plan the source-native SQL it pushes down. Nothing physical crosses between Purchase and Customer.
The two models link on Customer and Time. When a question needs both (for example top spenders in Wisconsin pulls state from address and spend from purchase ), Mosaic pushes the appropriate aggregation to each source and combines the results on the linking attributes. No ETL, no third copy.
Domain ownership follows the model boundary. The CRM team owns Customer, and the data system team owns Purchase. Neither hands over its source. They agree on the linking attributes, and security propagates from the underlying models automatically. There’s no materialized cross-engine join and no shared physical schema between Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora. The join is the linking-attribute agreement.
Attributes and hierarchies
Attributes carry multiple forms. Customer uses cid as the ID form and first_name + last_name as the display form, so an agent can ask about “Carolyn Inworth” and Mosaic resolves it to the right key on both sides of the link. Figure 2 shows the Customer attribute authored in Mosaic Studio, with cid as the ID form and Full Name, First Name, and Last Name as display forms.

Figure 2: Customer attribute definition in Design Center. cid is the ID form used to join on the underlying key. Full Name, First Name, and Last Name are display forms.

Two hierarchies matter for C360:

The Category hierarchy rolls up through parent to Department. The category.parent self-reference means a department-level question aggregates consistently.
Address rolls up through City to State in the same pattern. That makes State = 'WI' a single attribute qualification rather than a join the agent must construct.

Figure 3 shows the geography hierarchy authored in Design Center, chaining State through City and ZIP Code down to Customer.

Figure 3: Geography hierarchy in Design Center for the Customer model. State rolls up through City and ZIP Code to Location, and Location links to Customer.

The agent asks for State = 'WI' , not for address.state . Physical column names don’t leave the model. Every consumer of the semantic layer sees the attribute form and its display forms, and the hierarchy carries the rollup automatically.
Metrics: Base, advanced, compound, time-intelligence
A base metric applies a group function to a fact. Purchase Amount is Sum(price * quantity) on the purchase table.
Figure 4 shows the Purchase Amount base metric authored in Mosaic Studio: the formula Price * Quantity, with a description field that tells the agent what the metric means in business terms.

Figure 4: Purchase Amount metric authored in Design Center. The formula multiplies price by quantity, and the description tells the agent what the metric means in business terms.

The interesting C360 concepts are advanced metrics: an aggregation qualified by a named condition. In Strategy, conditions are references to filter objects in angle brackets, not inline predicates. Filter objects are model objects with their own name, description, and permissions, so they are reusable and auditable across metrics that share a definition.
Define the filters once:

Filter object
Qualification

[Large Orders]
Purchase Amount > 500

[Sports Category]
Category = "Sports"

[Rewards Members]
Rewards Account is not null

[Card Present]
Purchase Card is not null

[Big Spender]
Customer Lifetime Spend > 10000

Each filter object carries a name, description, qualification, and access permissions. The shape a modeler authors or exports for [Large Orders] looks like this:

name: [Large Orders]
description: Purchases whose net line amount exceeds $500.
Referenced by Large Order Spend and any metric that
scopes to high-value transactions.
qualification: Purchase Amount > 500
permissions: read: Everyone
modify: Data Modelers

Then reference the filters in metric expressions. Each of these is an advanced metric: a base aggregation qualified by a named filter.

Large Order Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} <[Large Orders]>
Sports Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} <[Sports Category]>
Rewards Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} <[Rewards Members]>

Figure 5 shows the Design Center view of an advanced metric with a filter condition applied. It uses the same authoring pattern as the preceding Large Order Spend .

Figure 5: Advanced-metric authoring in Design Center, showing the base formula and the filter condition referenced from the Large Orders filter object.

Customer Lifetime Spend also needs a level qualifier, because lifetime means the whole history regardless of how the current question is sliced:

Customer Lifetime Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+, !Customer+}

The ! before Customer sets grouping to none, so the metric returns each customer’s full total on every row rather than collapsing to one row per customer. See Strategy Metric Level Symbols for the full syntax.
Notice that [Big Spender] in the filter table qualifies on a metric expression rather than an attribute predicate. Filter objects can gate on either. Share of wallet is a compound metric, built from other metrics:

Sports Share of Wallet [Sports Spend] / [Customer Lifetime Spend]

Levels and conditions carry through from the components unchanged. Share of wallet is a ratio, so it doesn’t add or average. The share across an AWS Region isn’t the average of each customer’s share, and the metric description tells the agent that. See Strategy Conditional Metrics .
Beyond base, advanced, and compound, Mosaic ships governed time-intelligence metrics as first-class expressions. Previous Year , Previous Quarter , Year-to-Date , and Quarter-to-Date are declared once on the model and preserved through slice, so a question like how does Sports spend this year compare with last year becomes an attribute pick and two metric references rather than a hand-written SQL date filter. Custom calendars attach at the model level, so the same year-over-year expression works for a fiscal year that ends in September and a calendar year that ends in December. See Governed Time-Intelligence Metrics in Mosaic .
Edit the filter object once and the Power BI dashboard, the SQL extract, and the agent all move together. That is what a named, governed model artifact gets you that an inline SQL predicate cannot.
How Mosaic plans and executes queries
The Mosaic engine parses each MCP query call as Trino-dialect SQL, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying Purchase and Customer models, applies the RLS or OLS that the caller is subject to, and plans physical SQL per source. The dialect matches what Strategy publishes for the MCP query tool , so the SQL the agent emits is portable across MCP clients connecting to the same certified model.
For the auto-enrollment question, planning unfolds like this:

Push down to Amazon Aurora: a join of customer and rewards_account on cid , projecting profile and rewards_account.create_date , filtered where enrollment is null. Returns one row per unenrolled customer.
Push down to Amazon Redshift: SUM(price * quantity) grouped by cid . Returns one row per customer with total spend.
Combine inside Mosaic: join the two intermediate result sets on cid (the linking attribute), rank by lifetime spend, and return the top 20.

Aurora runs a transactional profile join. Amazon Redshift runs the fact aggregation. Mosaic handles the cross-engine join on a small intermediate set (one row per customer, not one row per order). A hand-written pipeline approximates the same shape and then must be kept in sync forever.
One SQL detail matters. Metrics are governed values, but Trino treats them as selected columns, so when a query uses GROUP BY , metrics need an aggregation wrapper such as SUM(metric_name) . The metric’s definition, conditions, and join paths are still resolved by Mosaic. The outer aggregation is the caller’s. A non-additive ratio like share of wallet therefore needs to say so in its description.
Live pushdown or in-memory
Every Mosaic model runs in one of two modes.

Mode
Behavior
Best fit

Live
Pushdown to Redshift or Aurora at query time
Consistently-current data. Source security applies directly

In-memory
Answered from a Mosaic-resident cube
Bounded recent windows. Predictable latency. No per-query warehouse compute

Both modes enforce the same security rules. RLS and OLS are set once on the model and evaluated regardless of where the answer comes from. The choice is a performance and cost question.
Agent traffic is repetitive and bursty. An agent decomposing top spenders in Wisconsin into several exploratory follow-ups fires many small queries over the same recent slice. Serving that from memory turns variable per-query warehouse spend into fixed Mosaic capacity, and it’s usually faster. For interactive agent workloads over a bounded window, in-memory is often both quicker and cheaper. Configure Mosaic-side entitlements before switching a model to in-memory, and validate them in the same test pass you use to validate the numbers.
One definition, four interfaces
The metrics, attributes, hierarchies, and security rules built in the previous section reach every consumer through native protocols. No connector translation, no metric re-implementation, no drift.

Protocol
Typical consumer
What it uses Mosaic for

MCP
AI agents (Strands, Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini)
Semantic discovery + governed query

SQL / JDBC / ODBC (Trino)
Tableau, SQL clients, Python notebooks
Flexibility and ad-hoc analysis

DAX / XMLA
Power BI, Excel PivotTables
Semantic fidelity for BI

REST
Custom applications, data science
Programmatic access

The same certified Mosaic model that the Strands agent in this walkthrough consumes also serves a business analyst working in Amazon Quick , which registers Mosaic MCP as an OAuth-authenticated connector. No second integration is required.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Mosaic enforces access in the semantic layer, before a query reaches Amazon Redshift or Aurora. HR and fraud roles see personally identifiable information (PII) fields like ssn and card_num . Marketing and analytics roles do not. Enforcement is identical whether the caller is a Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One set of RLS and OLS objects, one certified-model gate, one privilege check. Attributes and metrics marked as sensitive also feed Mosaic Sentinel Risk Management , which alerts on queries that touch flagged objects and detects behavioral anomalies as a defense-in-depth layer next to OLS.
Figure 6 shows the identity propagation chain across two lanes: the front-door OAuth handshake that runs once per user, and the per-request path that runs on every agent tool call. Each lane carries the user’s identity end-to-end so Mosaic can enforce RLS and OLS on the caller rather than a service account.

Figure 6: Identity propagation chain. The front-door OAuth handshake runs once per user, or on refresh-token renewal (steps 1-4). The per-request path runs on every agent tool call (steps 5-10). Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Mosaic evaluates governance on the caller’s Strategy user identity.

The chain follows two lanes.
Front-door OAuth handshake (once per user). The human user authenticates against the enterprise IdP. The application starts an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow against Strategy Library at /collaboration/authorize with scope offline_access . Strategy Library, federated to the same IdP through SAML or OIDC, returns a refresh and access token pair at /collaboration/token . The app persists the refresh token to AWS Secrets Manager, keyed by the user’s IdP sub claim.
Per-request path (every agent tool call). AgentCore Gateway validates the IdP JWT and routes to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent invoking Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. The agent’s MCP tool retrieves the user’s refresh token from Secrets Manager, exchanges it for a fresh access token, and presents Authorization: Bearer <access_token> to /collaboration/mcp/mosaic . Mosaic resolves the token to a Strategy user, enforces the Use MCP Server privilege, certified-model gate, and RLS and OLS, then plans and executes against Purchase and Customer. A marketing analyst doesn’t see ssn or card_num . A fraud analyst does.
Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Governance evaluates on the caller’s identity from IdP to Mosaic engine.
Expose the layer through the Mosaic MCP server
Strategy Library exposes two MCP endpoints:

Endpoint
Path
What it does

Agents MCP
/collaboration/mcp/agent
Routes a question to a certified Strategy agent, which answers using its own data and instructions

Mosaic MCP
/collaboration/mcp/mosaic
Queries Mosaic models and AI-enabled cubes directly, no Strategy agent required

Both work independently. This walkthrough uses Mosaic MCP . Putting the semantic layer directly in front of the Strands agent skips an inference hop.
The tool chain
Four tools, chained from project to model to semantics to query.

Tool
What it does
Parameters

get_projects
Lists Strategy projects the caller can access
none

get_models
Lists certified Mosaic models and datasets in a project
project

get_semantics
Returns a model’s full definition: attributes and metrics with data types, descriptions, and metric formulas
model

query
Runs a read-only Trino SQL query. Writes and DDL rejected with MOSAIC_SQL_WRITE_REJECTED
sql

The agent chains these calls automatically. get_projects and get_models narrow to the right model by description before the agent reads a column name. get_semantics returns the governed definitions the agent then uses to compose SQL against real object names: Sports Share of Wallet as a compound metric, Customer Lifetime Spend scoped to Customer, the Category hierarchy, and the formula for every metric.
Two Mosaic-specific SQL conventions matter. Column identifiers follow a <form>__<name> pattern and must be wrapped in double quotes ( "customer__customer name" ). Time attributes are exposed both as base columns and as pre-bucketed interval columns ( (day interval) , (month interval) ), and the docs explicitly say to use the interval columns for time-grouped aggregations rather than date_trunc .
Metadata is what makes it accurate
get_semantics returns definitions, but the agent still must choose the right metric. Without descriptions, Total Spend and Customer Lifetime Spend look interchangeable, and they aren’t. Four properties do most of the work: object descriptions (what the metric means and when not to use it, including aggregation behavior for non-additive metrics), semantic definitions (how compound metrics compose), relationships (which attributes are valid slices), and governance context (so the agent can say what it can’t see rather than presenting a filtered number as complete). The model description is the first thing get_models returns and it’s how the agent picks the right model. Mosaic can import metadata from upstream catalogs, so column descriptions already maintained flow in rather than being retyped.
Deploy the agent
Strands is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the Mosaic MCP endpoint as a tool source. The AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and forwards the human user’s JWT.
The system prompt matters. Give the agent explicit instructions to follow the three-step call pattern before writing SQL: get_projects , then get_models , then get_semantics on the target model. Tell it to reference only attribute and metric names that get_semantics returned. Include a short section on the business terminology in the target model ( Customer Lifetime Spend is the customer’s total across their history regardless of the current slice. Sports Share of Wallet is a ratio. And so on). This is the prompt engineering that pays the most in accuracy.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The get_semantics payload runs to a few thousand tokens and doesn’t change within a model version, so caching drops the input-token cost per call on repeated invocations. Agent traffic against a stable semantic layer is exactly the repetitive, bursty pattern that benefits most.
Two effects compound on the MCP path. First, get_semantics returns compressed business context (metric definitions, hierarchies, attribute forms) instead of raw schema DDL, so the model reasons over a smaller, higher-signal payload. Strategy’s published benchmark measures the input-token and per-query cost impact of serving semantic context versus raw schema. Second, Bedrock prompt caching keeps that already-compressed payload warm across calls. For repetitive agent traffic, both effects apply per call: the model reasons over compressed context, and repeat calls hit the cache.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three query categories through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them as a different role.
Query 1, Aurora-only. List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.
The agent generates a query against the Customer model that projects the display forms of Customer and City and filters state to WI:

SELECT "customer__customer name", "city__city name"
FROM "Customer"
WHERE "state__state name" = 'WI'
ORDER BY "customer__customer name"

Mosaic pushes a single query to Aurora and returns the rows. Amazon Redshift is not touched.
Query 2, Amazon Redshift only. What are our top 10 products by units sold?

SELECT "product__product name", SUM("Units Sold") AS "total_units"
FROM "Purchase"
GROUP BY "product__product name"
ORDER BY "total_units" DESC
LIMIT 10

The entire query pushes to Amazon Redshift. Aurora is not touched.
Query 3, cross-model. Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?

SELECT "customer__customer name",
"state__state name",
SUM("Customer Lifetime Spend") AS "lifetime_spend"
FROM "Customer"
WHERE "rewards_account__account_id" IS NULL
GROUP BY "customer__customer name", "state__state name"
ORDER BY "lifetime_spend" DESC
LIMIT 20

Mosaic plans across both models. Profile and enrollment status come from Aurora, spend aggregation from Amazon Redshift, joined on the Customer linking attribute inside the Mosaic engine, then filtered and top-N’d. The agent did not need to define Customer Lifetime Spend . It referenced the metric by name and Mosaic resolved the formula, level qualifier, and linking paths.
Governance rerun. We ran Query 1 with ssn added to the projection as two callers. As a fraud analyst, get_semantics returned the SSN attribute and the query returned the values. As a marketing analyst, get_semantics returned a Customer attribute without ssn at all, so the agent had no attribute to project. Same request, same query text, two correct answers from one definition.
Cross-interface confirmation. We opened the same certified Customer model in Excel through the Mosaic XMLA endpoint and dragged State and Customer Lifetime Spend onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals matched the agent’s numbers exactly.
Early in the run, the agent averaged share of wallet across customers, the classic non-additive mistake. Adding one line to the metric description ( “ratio metric. Do not average across customers, recompute from components” ) stopped it. That’s the case for writing metric descriptions in the first sprint rather than the last.
Extending across data sources
The same linking mechanism extends to a third source: clickstream events in Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ) queried through Amazon Athena, tables in Apache Iceberg on Amazon S3 Tables , a capability of Amazon S3, or a SaaS source such as a CRM. Model the source in Mosaic, link it on Customer and Time, and browse-to-buy questions compose into the same customer view without a third pipeline. Adding a source doesn’t change the metric definitions that already exist. The agent can only travel paths a modeler declared. AWS Lake Formation governs access to the underlying lake tables. Mosaic’s RLS and OLS apply on top.
The same live-source pattern applies to every system in Strategy’s supported data source catalog , covering on-premises databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL alongside the warehouses and engines already named in this post.
Interoperability with Apache Ossie
Some tools will not take a dependency on a single semantic layer. Apache Ossie (incubating) is the open specification for that gap, launched as the Open Semantic Interchange on September 23, 2025 and now in the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie (incubating). It defines a vendor-neutral format for metrics, dimensions, relationships, and business concepts so definitions move between tools without being retyped. Strategy participates alongside Snowflake, Dremio, dbt Labs, Salesforce, and others.
Mosaic exports and imports Ossie artifacts. Metric and dimension definitions modeled over Amazon Redshift publish as Ossie YAML consumable by Ossie-aware tools without a Mosaic connector. Definitions authored elsewhere (a metric maintained in dbt, a dimension standardized in a catalog) flow into Mosaic instead of being re-implemented. The artifacts are plain text, so they live in Git and promote through environments like other code.
Apache Ossie is early. Use it where portability matters most and fidelity matters least, for example formulas, dimensions, descriptions, and ownership metadata, while keeping governance policy, execution strategy, and security configuration native to Mosaic.
Deployment: Strategy Cloud
Mosaic runs as a managed service on Strategy Cloud. Strategy operates the application. Connections to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora go over the network from Strategy Cloud egress. You allow-list the Strategy Cloud CIDRs on the source security groups.
Observability
Two observability planes cover the path from question to answer.
Sentinel and Platform Analytics cover the query side. Sentinel captures near real-time query duration, slow queries, and usage by user, tool, and model.
AgentCore Observability , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, covers the agent side: planning steps, tool calls, latency per turn. Sentinel and Platform Analytics show what happened once the request reached Mosaic. AgentCore Observability shows what the agent was doing before it got there.
Conclusion
Reliable agentic analytics combines strong reasoning, trusted business context, and secure execution. Amazon Bedrock provides the model, Strategy Mosaic provides the governed semantic layer over live data, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent and terminates authentication. The agent talks to the semantic layer, not to Amazon Redshift or Aurora directly. Schemas evolve, the semantic model absorbs the change, and the same definitions serve Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, the Strands agent, and Amazon Quick. Through Apache Ossie, they also reach tools that do not connect to Mosaic.
Where to start

Pick one metric currently argued about (NRR, contribution margin, active customer are common candidates). One metric with more than one definition in circulation.
Write three to five business questions about it. These become your acceptance tests.
Model your primary source in Mosaic and get the metric returning a defensible number.
Link additional sources incrementally, one at a time, on the attributes that already exist in the model.
Author descriptions on every metric and attribute the agent will see. This is where accuracy moves most.
Connect the Strands agent over Mosaic MCP and run your acceptance questions.
Observe real query patterns for a couple of weeks, then move what’s hot to in-memory.
Export stable definitions to Apache Ossie and put them under version control.
